name: Edge lift (one arm, loading pin)
technique: Technique as taught for arm-lifting (block pulls): arm straight and resting against the front of the hip, the block hanging in front of the body between the legs, back straight, the lift driven by straightening the knees, no shrug or row (a loading pin that is too long forces a shrug). Lift, hold the block about 2–3 seconds (peak finger force builds in about 1–1.5 s), set it down. The fingers keep their grip throughout; in a half crimp an index finger straightening out of its ~90° bend is the cue to stop the set. A cord through both sides of the block keeps the edge level, as modelled here; a cord through one side tilts it like an incut, which this model doesn't cover. Strong climbers lift far more than the 100% strength default (taken from recreational climbers): use the strength slider. Source: StrengthClimbing's arm-lifting guide (see References, resources).
angleNote: The edge lift is a static hold: the fingers keep one position while the block comes up, so nothing moves at the finger joints. The slider doesn't animate a lift; it compares holds with the middle joint (PIP) at different angles: 0° = straight, about 90° = half crimp, about 105° = full crimp. Each grip keeps its own fingertip (DIP) and knuckle (MCP) angles and starts at its measured position.

finger.label: Index finger
finger.lengthsNote: Bone lengths in metres, mean of 7 index fingers. The middle finger, which carries the most load on an edge, is somewhat longer; scale with care.
finger.lengthsSource: An KN, Ueba Y, Chao EY, Cooney WP, Linscheid RL (1983). Tendon excursion and moment arm of index finger muscles. J Biomech 16(6):419–425. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(83)90074-X (Table 1)
finger.momentArmsNote: Flexion moment arms in metres, averaged through each joint's range (7 index fingers). Table 3 is headed mm but its values are in cm: Table 2's excursions per 100° (e.g. FDP at the DIP 7.30 mm → 4.2 mm per radian) confirm it. The paper notes they grow slightly with flexion; Schweizer measured much more bowstringing over the PIP in the crimp, so the PIP moment arms are probably too small there (overestimating the tensions).
finger.momentArmsSource: An KN, Ueba Y, Chao EY, Cooney WP, Linscheid RL (1983). Tendon excursion and moment arm of index finger muscles. J Biomech 16(6):419–425. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(83)90074-X (Tables 2 and 3)
finger.bowstringNote: Extra distance (m) of the flexor tendons from the bone over the PIP under load, added to the PIP moment arms. Measured over the PIP: FDP 0.2 mm in the slope grip (PIP 0–10°) and 4.3 mm in the crimp (PIP 90°); FDS alone 1.75 mm in the crimp. Linear in between and held flat beyond 90° (estimate). Taking the extra distance as extra moment arm is an approximation.
finger.bowstringSource: Schweizer A (2001). Biomechanical properties of the crimp grip position in rock climbers. J Biomech 34(2):217–223. doi:10.1016/S0021-9290(00)00184-6 (Table 1, position 4: over the PIP joint; 16 fingers)
finger.pulleysNote: A2 is 40.7% of the proximal phalanx long and sits at its mid-portion, so on this 43.6 mm phalanx its distal edge is 13 mm before the PIP; A4 sits at the middle of the middle phalanx. Tendon insertions (FDS 35% along the middle phalanx, FDP 30% along the distal phalanx) are estimates (TODO). Tendons run straight between them (bone-axis geometry, no tendon thickness).
finger.pulleysSource: Lin GT, Amadio PC, An KN, Cooney WP (1989). Functional anatomy of the human digital flexor pulley system. J Hand Surg Am 14(6):949–956 (Table III: A2 40.7%, A4 13.0% of the proximal phalanx's length, index finger extended); mid-portion of the phalanges: Lin GT, Cooney WP, Amadio PC, An KN (1990). Mechanical properties of human pulleys. J Hand Surg Br 15(4):429–434
finger.pulleyStrengthNote: Breaking load in newtons, index finger (mean of 5 cadaver hands, Table 1; middle finger A2 466 N, A4 210 N; all fingers A2 407 N, A4 210 N). Measured with a hook pulling straight across the pulley in cadavers, so living, trained climbers' pulleys may differ; a guide to scale, not a safety limit.
finger.pulleyStrengthSource: Lin GT, Cooney WP, Amadio PC, An KN (1990). Mechanical properties of human pulleys. J Hand Surg Br 15(4):429–434 (Table 1)
finger.contactNote: Where the edge presses: the centre of the pressure on the distal phalanx, measured from the DIP. Default half the distal phalanx, as Vigouroux et al. assumed for their 1 cm hold. On a 20–25 mm edge the whole distal phalanx and pad rest on the edge; where the centre then sits hasn't been measured (TODO), so it is a slider: closer to the DIP means less FDP and more FDS.
finger.contactSource: Vigouroux L, Quaine F, Labarre-Vila A, Moutet F (2006). Estimation of finger muscle tendon tensions and pulley forces during specific sport-climbing grip techniques. J Biomech 39(14):2583–2592. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.08.027 (Methods 2.2)
finger.crossCheck: Direction checked against surface EMG in maximal two-arm dead-hangs (25 climbers, similar loads in both grips): the crimp (PIP about 90°) showed 17% more FDS activity than the slope grip, and no significant FDP difference. The model, at equal load: half crimp vs open hand, FDS about 3.6×, FDP about 1.3×. Same direction; raw surface EMG isn't proportional to tendon force (and picks up neighbouring muscles), so the sizes can't be compared.
finger.crossCheckSource: Ferrer-Uris B, Arias D, Torrado P, Marina M, Busquets A (2023). Exploring forearm muscle coordination and training applications of various grip positions during maximal isometric finger dead-hangs in rock climbers. PeerJ 11:e15464. doi:10.7717/peerj.15464 (Table 2; CC BY 4.0)
finger.referenceTensionNote: Tendon tension at a maximal one-finger effort (highest group mean of the two grips: FDP in the crimp, FDS in the slope grip), used to scale the muscle bars.
finger.referenceTensionSource: Vigouroux L, Quaine F, Labarre-Vila A, Moutet F (2006). Estimation of finger muscle tendon tensions and pulley forces during specific sport-climbing grip techniques. J Biomech 39(14):2583–2592. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.08.027 (Table 3)

friction.note: Contact rule: pad and edge are both curved and touch where their surfaces face each other. The pad's surface faces the distal phalanx's palm side ± 35° (estimate); the edge's runs from its top face (tilted by the face-angle slider) round the lip to its front. The contact normal is the shared direction nearest the push; needed coefficient = tan(angle between push and contact normal). Constant coefficient: on rough holds the pad's friction hardly depends on load, because above about 2 N its contact area stops growing.
friction.source: Li FX, Margetts S, Fowler I (2001). Use of 'chalk' in rock climbing: sine qua non or myth? J Sports Sci 19(6):427–432 (fingertip on rock, maximum static coefficient 2.5–3.3; chalk lowered it); Fuss FK, Weizman Y, Niegl G, Tan AM (2020). Climbers' perception of hold surface properties: roughness versus slip resistance. Front Psychol 11:252 (coefficient climbers used on an instrumented hold: averages 0.56–0.86 by surface; a 29° sloping surface needs at least 0.55); load independence on rough surfaces: Dzidek BM, Adams MJ, Andrews JW, Zhang Z, Johnson SA (2017). Contact mechanics of the human finger pad under compressive loads. J R Soc Interface 14(127):20160935. doi:10.1098/rsif.2016.0935; coefficient used while hanging: Kilgas MA, Drum SN, Jensen RL, Phillips KC, Watts PB (2016). The effect of magnesium carbonate (chalk) on geometric entropy, force, and electromyography during rock climbing. J Appl Biomech 32(6):553–557. doi:10.1123/jab.2016-0009 (19 climbers, hang to failure on one hold); contact area and the two-term friction law: Adams MJ, Johnson SA, Lefèvre P, Lévesque V, Hayward V, André T, Thonnard JL (2013). Finger pad friction and its role in grip and touch. J R Soc Interface 10(80):20120467. doi:10.1098/rsif.2012.0467

finger.strengthCheck: Strength scale: 100% = recreational climbers (the reference tensions and fingertip forces). Hang tests put stronger climbers well above it: climbers around French 7a held 133% of body mass in a two-arm hang on 21 mm (this model: about 125–150%), intermediate to elite climbers about 80–85% of body mass one-armed on 20 mm (this model: about 115% for the women's mean, 160% for the men's in the half crimp; the open hand comes out relatively weaker here than measured). One-hand lifts like this one, standing on a force plate (15 experienced climbers, crimp): about 393 N (40 kg; range 27–58 kg) on a 12.5 mm edge (this model at 100%: 38 kg half crimp, 31–33 kg open hand and full crimp), but only about 283 / 240 / 185 / 110 N on 7.3 / 5.8 / 4.3 / 2.8 mm edges, and the shallow-edge forces didn't follow the deep-edge ones: there the fingertip's pulp, not strength, sets the limit (not modelled).
finger.strengthCheckSource: Ferrer-Uris B, Arias D, Torrado P, Marina M, Busquets A (2023). Exploring forearm muscle coordination and training applications of various grip positions during maximal isometric finger dead-hangs in rock climbers. PeerJ 11:e15464 (Table 2); Torr O, Randall T, Knowles R, Giles D, Atkins S (2022). Reliability and validity of a method for the assessment of sport rock climbers' isometric finger strength. J Strength Cond Res 36(8):2277–2282 (Table 2); Bourne R, Halaki M, Vanwanseele B, Clarke J (2011). Measuring lifting forces in rock climbing: effect of hold size and fingertip structure. J Appl Biomech 27(1):40–46. doi:10.1123/jab.27.1.40 (Fig. 4, read off; 15 experienced climbers, one hand, crimp grip, sandstone edges)

fingers.note: All four fingers on one edge. The fingertips line up on the edge (each pad may sit up to 6 mm deeper or shallower than the middle finger's); every finger keeps close to the grip's PIP and fingertip angles and takes up its length at the knuckle, the ring and little finger also by cupping the palm, and the whole hand may tilt sideways at the wrist (radial/ulnar deviation, −15° to +25°). Where the edge sits under the hand and the hand's tilt are chosen so the four postures together stay closest to the grip (weighted squared angle changes; weights are estimates). Moment arms are An et al.'s index-finger values scaled by each finger's proximal phalanx length (estimate). How the block splits between the fingers isn't fixed by statics: it is shared for least effort (smallest sum of squared tendon tension ÷ reference tension over each finger's FDP and FDS), with the FDP slips of the middle, ring and little finger pulled towards equal relative tension by the quadriga slider. A finger that only just reaches fades out of the split.
fingers.lengthsNote: Bone lengths in metres (means of 10 hands). The phalanges are used as measured; the knuckle line comes from knuckleBack, not from the metacarpal lengths.
fingers.lengthsSource: Lin GT, Amadio PC, An KN, Cooney WP (1989). Functional anatomy of the human digital flexor pulley system. J Hand Surg Am 14(6):949–956 (Table I: bone lengths of 10 hands; Table III: A2 length as a share of the proximal phalanx)
fingers.knuckleBackNote: How far each knuckle (MCP joint) sits back towards the wrist from the middle finger's, in metres, with the fingers in line with the hand. Sets the knuckle line; the wrist-to-knuckle distance is the middle metacarpal's length minus this. The metacarpal bone lengths alone would put the little finger's knuckle 12 mm back and the index's 3 mm ahead of the middle's, but the metacarpal bases don't sit level in the wrist. Estimate (TODO: measured knuckle positions, e.g. from a musculoskeletal hand model); users can enter their own.
fingers.mcpRangeNote: Active range of each knuckle (MCP) in degrees, extension negative: means of 31 healthy adults with the wrist in neutral (an edge lift holds the wrist near neutral). The reach search keeps every finger inside it. The small finger extends furthest, which helps it reach.
fingers.mcpRangeSource: Latz D, Koukos C, Boeckers P, Jungbluth P, Schiffner E, Kaufmann R, Gehrmann SV (2019). Influence of wrist position on the metacarpophalangeal joint motion of the index through small finger. Hand 14(2):259–263. doi:10.1177/1558944717736823 (Table 1, neutral wrist)
fingers.cmcFlexMaxNote: How far each metacarpal can bend forward at the base of the hand (degrees) to help a short finger reach: index and middle are nearly rigid, ring and little more mobile (cupping the palm). Estimates (TODO: anatomical source).
fingers.knuckleSideNote: Sideways position of each knuckle from the middle of the wrist, in metres (thumb side positive): about 2 cm apart. Estimate (TODO).
fingers.a2LengthNote: A2 length as a share of the proximal phalanx (Lin et al. 1989, Table III, extended finger); A2 is centred on the phalanx.
fingers.a2LengthSource: Lin GT, Amadio PC, An KN, Cooney WP (1989). Functional anatomy of the human digital flexor pulley system. J Hand Surg Am 14(6):949–956 (Table I: bone lengths of 10 hands; Table III: A2 length as a share of the proximal phalanx)
fingers.pcsaNote: Physiological cross-sectional area in cm² per finger (FDS index: both bellies combined). The little finger's FDS is tiny, so the little finger relies on its FDP.
fingers.pcsaSource: Lieber RL, Jacobson MD, Fazeli BM, Abrams RA, Botte MJ (1992). Architecture of selected muscles of the arm and forearm: anatomy and implications for tendon transfer. J Hand Surg Am 17(5):787–798 (Table I: physiological cross-sectional area of FDP and FDS per finger)
fingers.pulleyStrengthSource: Lin GT, Cooney WP, Amadio PC, An KN (1990). Mechanical properties of human pulleys. J Hand Surg Br 15(4):429–434 (Table 1: breaking load per finger)

arm.note: The arm holding the block: straight from shoulder to grip, the block hanging from the hand. Arm resting on the front of the hip with the block hanging between the legs: the load line runs (nearly) through elbow and shoulder, which are only pulled apart; the hip carries the arm's slight slant. The forward and sideways angles are measured from that resting position. Turned forward or out to the side: the block acts on a lever (arm length × sine of the angle), held by the shoulder flexors or abductors; the elbow, kept straight, is pushed towards over-straightening and held by the locked joint and the elbow flexors. Lengths and segment masses from the shared body data; forward and sideways reach combine as offsets (small-angle approximation).

shoulderFlexion.source: Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shape); Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1021105 (peak torque)

shoulderAbduction.note: As in the lateral raise: weakest with the arm down (62%).
shoulderAbduction.source: Haidar SG, Lloyd J, Cox D, Deshmukh S (2009). Shoulder abduction strength: is it affected by the degree of abduction? J Bone Joint Surg Br 91-B Suppl I:160 (conference abstract). doi:10.1302/0301-620X.91BSUPP_I.0910160c; Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Normal values of isokinetic maximum strength, the strength/velocity curve, and the angle at peak torque of all degrees of freedom in the shoulder. Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1021105; Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (Clarke et al., contrary finding at 0°)

elbowStraight.note: Elbow flexors with the arm straight: the curl's peak (65 Nm) × its curve at the lowest measured angle (32°, 0.52), held flat to 0° (extrapolation). The locked elbow joint also resists over-straightening passively, so this effort is an upper bound.
elbowStraight.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001

placement.label: Load
options: Block lift (block hanging from one hand)
placement.hint: The fingers don't know what pulls on the arm: the edge's push runs from the pad towards the wrist either way, so the finger loads follow from the force on the hand. Block lift: the block. Hang: body weight less what the feet carry, plus the added weight (the load slider), shared by the hands. In a hang the arm is overhead and only pulls, so the arm view and Play are off.

placement.label: Hands on the edge (hang)
placement.hint: Hang only: how many hands share the body weight.

placement.label: Weight on the feet (hang)
placement.hint: Hang only: the share of body weight the feet carry (0 = a free hang; feet on a box or the wall take the rest).

placement.label: Where the edge presses (from the fingertip joint)
placement.hint: Closer to the fingertip joint: more of the finger on the edge (a deeper edge). Further out: only the tip (a shallow edge). Where the pressure really centres isn't measured.

placement.label: Arm forward of the body
placement.hint: 0° = arm hanging against the front of the hip, as taught. Turning it forward puts the block on a lever at the shoulder.

placement.label: Arm out to the side
placement.hint: Sideways the shoulder abductors hold the lever; they are weakest with the arm down.

placement.label: Edge tilted along its length (+ = little-finger end lower)
placement.hint: A block hanging off-centre tilts the edge: the fingers at the lower end must reach further.

placement.label: Fingers on the edge
options: Auto (a finger that can't reach comfortably stays off)
placement.hint: On a flat edge the fingers' different lengths can't all be matched by one posture, least of all in an open hand, where the fingers are nearly straight: climbers then leave the index or the little finger off, or curl the longer fingers more. "All four" keeps every finger on whatever posture that takes (watch the knuckle angles); the edge-height bars or "Fits this hand" give the edge a profile instead.

placement.label: Edge face angle (+ = incut, − = sloping)
placement.hint: The face the pads press on, relative to square to the pull. An incut face pushes the pads deeper into the hold and needs no friction; a sloping face pushes them out, and every finger then needs at least tan(slope) (15°: μ 0.27). Fischer et al. measured their climbing postures on a 25° incut edge.

placement.label: Skin–edge friction (μ)
placement.hint: How much sideways force the pad can take per unit of pressing force before it slips. Pad and edge are both curved, so they touch where their surfaces face each other: a pad that can face the edge's top squarely needs no friction there; a fingertip that meets the edge steeply (open hand, the shorter little finger) touches the rounded lip, where part of the push runs along the pad. Measured values vary widely: fingertip on rock up to 2.5–3.3 at most (Li et al.), 0.56–0.86 actually used on gym-hold surfaces (Fuss et al.), only 0.37–0.38 while hanging on to failure, with or without chalk (Kilgas et al.). On rough holds skin friction hardly depends on the pressing force (Dzidek et al.); on smooth or moist surfaces it falls as the force rises (not modelled here).

placement.label: FDP of middle, ring and little finger linked (quadriga)
placement.hint: The deep flexor's slips to these three fingers share one muscle belly. 0% = each slip works on its own; 100% = one belly, every slip at the same share of its strength. How tightly they are linked on an edge isn't measured: 50% is a middle guess.

placement.label: Lift-off and set-down time (Play)
placement.hint: How quickly the block comes off the floor (5 cm) and back down. Quicker = a higher force peak at lift-off and touch-down, the same force while holding.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
muscles.note: Bends the fingertip. On an edge it carries the DIP moment alone, so its tension is set directly by the statics.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis
muscles.note: Bends the middle joint (PIP). Takes whatever PIP moment the FDP doesn't already supply: much more of it in a crimp.

phases.name: Open
phases.text: Finger fairly straight. The tendons run close to the bone, so the pulleys carry little; the fingertip (DIP) and FDP do most of the work.

phases.name: Half crimp
phases.text: The PIP bends towards 90°. The flexor tendons bowstring across the PIP and pull hard on the A2 and A4 pulleys; the FDS takes a larger share.

phases.name: Crimp
phases.text: PIP past 90°: the sharpest bend for the tendons, the highest pulley loads per newton at the fingertip.

variants.name: Open hand (drag)
variants.equipment: Edge block on a loading pin
variants.notes: Middle joint moderately bent, fingertip about straight, knuckles nearly straight: MCP 4°, PIP 54°, DIP 1°, measured with motion capture in elite climbers on a 23 mm edge (middle finger, mean of both hands). The open hand varied most between climbers (PIP −4° to 82°), in two patterns that the authors link to whether the little finger is on the hold; the ring finger stayed straighter (PIP about 25°). Vigouroux et al.'s 'slope' grip, with the knuckles bent back and the middle joint nearly straight (MCP −21°, PIP 26°, DIP 39°), is the PIP slider's low end. The A2 pulley carries about half the full crimp's load per newton at the fingertip; in the flat slope grip it would carry far less.
variants.source: Posture: Fischer G, Schneeberger M, Petter SA, Scheibler AG, Wolf P, Calcagni M, Schweizer A, Reissner L (2024). Motion analysis of the wrist and finger joints in sport climbing. Bioengineering 11(4):370. doi:10.3390/bioengineering11040370 (Table 5: middle finger, holding phase, mean of both hands; CC BY 4.0); for comparison, the slope grip: Vigouroux L, Quaine F, Labarre-Vila A, Moutet F (2006). Estimation of finger muscle tendon tensions and pulley forces during specific sport-climbing grip techniques. J Biomech 39(14):2583–2592. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.08.027; maximum fingertip force (all four fingers on the hold, slope grip, 78 N): Schweizer A (2001). Biomechanical properties of the crimp grip position in rock climbers. J Biomech 34(2):217–223. doi:10.1016/S0021-9290(00)00184-6

variants.name: Half crimp
variants.equipment: Edge block on a loading pin
variants.notes: Middle joint well bent, fingertip slightly bent back, knuckles a little bent: MCP 14°, PIP 72°, DIP −12°, measured with motion capture in elite climbers on a 23 mm edge (middle finger, mean of both hands). Climbers ranged widely (PIP 28° to 87°); many 'half crimps' are flatter than the 90° often quoted. The maximum force is taken from the crimp. A grip between half crimp and open hand with all four fingers is often recommended for off-the-wall strength training (Tyler Nelson, via StrengthClimbing); in the 'chisel' variant the index finger stays straight and carries little.
variants.source: Posture: Fischer G, Schneeberger M, Petter SA, Scheibler AG, Wolf P, Calcagni M, Schweizer A, Reissner L (2024). Motion analysis of the wrist and finger joints in sport climbing. Bioengineering 11(4):370. doi:10.3390/bioengineering11040370 (Table 5: middle finger, holding phase, mean of both hands; CC BY 4.0); maximum fingertip force (all four fingers on the hold, crimp, 82 N): Schweizer A (2001). Biomechanical properties of the crimp grip position in rock climbers. J Biomech 34(2):217–223. doi:10.1016/S0021-9290(00)00184-6

variants.name: Full crimp
variants.equipment: Edge block on a loading pin
variants.notes: Middle joint sharply bent, fingertip bent back, knuckles clearly bent: MCP 40°, PIP 87°, DIP −26°, measured with motion capture in elite climbers on a 23 mm edge (middle finger, mean of both hands). Vigouroux et al.'s crimp (MCP −3°, PIP 107°, DIP −23°) bends the middle joint further and keeps the knuckles straight; the model's check against their tendon estimates uses their posture. With the fingertip bent back, the joint itself carries about a fifth of the DIP moment (22% in their climbers), which spares the FDP. The thumb wrapped over the index finger isn't modelled.
variants.source: Posture: Fischer G, Schneeberger M, Petter SA, Scheibler AG, Wolf P, Calcagni M, Schweizer A, Reissner L (2024). Motion analysis of the wrist and finger joints in sport climbing. Bioengineering 11(4):370. doi:10.3390/bioengineering11040370 (Table 5: middle finger, holding phase, mean of both hands; CC BY 4.0); passive DIP moment and the check posture: Vigouroux L, Quaine F, Labarre-Vila A, Moutet F (2006). Estimation of finger muscle tendon tensions and pulley forces during specific sport-climbing grip techniques. J Biomech 39(14):2583–2592. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.08.027 (Table 2); maximum fingertip force (82 N): Schweizer A (2001). Biomechanical properties of the crimp grip position in rock climbers. J Biomech 34(2):217–223. doi:10.1016/S0021-9290(00)00184-6

handModel.note: The Muscles 3D view: bones and every muscle's path (pulleys and wrapping included) from the ARMS hand and wrist model at the three grips' preset postures (tools/arms_hand_export.py, OpenSim 4.6). NON-COMMERCIAL: the ARMS model is licensed for non-commercial use only, so this view and its data file (data/opensim/arms-hand.json) are not covered by the site's CC BY licence.

A musculoskeletal model of the hand and wrist capable of simulating functional tasks. bioRxiv 2021.12.28.474357 (ARMS hand and wrist model 4.3, simtk.org/projects/arms_hand_model; non-commercial licence)
